approved: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
This bill would create a new government body to invest $15 billion in Australian industry.
The National Reconstruction Fund Corporation would provide loans and buy equity in businesses in priority areas of the economy.
The Corporation's investment mandate would be set by ministers through a non-disallowable legislative instrument, while priority areas would be declared in a disallowable instrument.
Establishes the National Reconstruction Fund Corporation as a corporate Commonwealth entity.
Sets out the Corporation's investment functions, including providing financial accommodation and acquiring equity interests in priority areas.
Creates a special account for the Corporation's funding and allows ministers to issue an Investment Mandate.
Australian industry and businesses in priority areas of the economy.

According to [Odgers' Australian Senate Practice](https://www.aph.gov.au/About_Parliament/Senate/Powers_practice_n_procedures/Odgers_Australian_Senate_Practice/Chapter_14#h08): > *The equivalent of adjourning consideration of a matter in committee of the whole is to report progress. The committee reports to the Senate that the committee has considered the matter referred to it, has made progress, and seeks leave to sit again at some future time for further consideration. The Senate then normally, by motion, gives the committee leave to sit again at a later time, and consideration of the matter in committee of the whole then becomes an order of the day for that later time.*

National Reconstruction Fund Corporation Bill 2023 - Consideration of Senate Message - Agree with the Senate amendments

Investment decisions of the $15 billion National Reconstruction Fund will be made solely by its board, with ministers required to consider listed skills criteria when appointing members. The minister rejected concerns about political stacking, cited the CEFC as a model, and criticised the opposition’s record on manufacturing.

The opposition will oppose the National Reconstruction Fund Corporation Bill 2022, arguing it does nothing for manufacturers and ignores their key concerns — citing a survey where 83% of manufacturers faced rising energy prices, and giving examples of Solaris Paper’s tripled gas bill and Advanced Bricks’ closure after 82 years.

A survey of Mackellar found integrity in politics remains the second most important issue; the MP supported the National Reconstruction Fund Corporation Bill but criticised clause 18 for allowing ministers to appoint board members, risking political influence over $11 billion in investment decisions.

The speaker argued that the National Reconstruction Fund Corporation Bill 2022 is essential for rebuilding Australia's manufacturing capacity and supply chain resilience after COVID-19, listing seven priority areas including medical science, renewables and defence. The opposition speaker criticised the $15 billion fund as an expensive, poorly designed intervention that bypasses parliamentary oversight, ignores energy price and labour shortages, and risks wasteful spending.

The Albanese government argued the $15 billion National Reconstruction Fund, a key election commitment, is necessary to rebuild Australia's manufacturing capability, create secure jobs, and strengthen supply chains after the pandemic exposed vulnerabilities. The opposition argued the bill lacks detail, risks driving inflation through off-budget spending, and gives inappropriate ministerial discretion, including appointing union officials to the board.

The Prime Minister argued for the National Reconstruction Fund to boost Australian manufacturing, jobs, and economic sovereignty, citing the Clean Energy Finance Corporation’s success in unlocking $2.60 in private investment per dollar and listing seven priority areas including renewables, medical science, and defence.

The National Reconstruction Fund Corporation Bill 2022 establishes a $15 billion fund to invest in seven priority areas—including renewables, medical science, transport, and defence—aiming to revitalise Australian manufacturing and create secure jobs. Coalition speakers opposed the bill, arguing it would increase union influence, ignore cost-of-living pressures, and duplicate existing programs like the Modern Manufacturing Initiative.

The speaker argued in support of the National Reconstruction Fund Corporation Bill 2022, a $15 billion investment in seven priority areas including renewables, medical science, transport, and defence, and criticised the opposition for opposing the bill. The speaker also referenced the opposition's past cuts of $50 billion from hospitals and their role in the departure of the Australian car industry.

The opposition argued the National Reconstruction Fund Corporation Bill 2022 is poorly designed, fiscally irresponsible, and prioritises union interests, claiming it ignores rising energy costs, labour shortages, and disrupted supply chains. They opposed the $15 billion off-budget fund, criticised the removal of space manufacturing as a priority, and defended the former coalition's Modern Manufacturing Strategy as superior.
The question was put on the National Reconstruction Fund Corporation Bill 2022 for a second reading, with no further debate allowed.

The bill establishes a $15 billion National Reconstruction Fund Corporation to invest in seven priority areas—value-add resources, agriculture, transport, medical science, renewables, defence, and enabling capabilities—with an independent board, aiming to rebuild Australia's industrial capability and create secure, well-paying jobs.

The Coalition opposed the National Reconstruction Fund Corporation Bill 2023, arguing it would fuel inflation and ignore manufacturers' needs for lower energy and input costs, citing the IMF's warning against off-budget spending and examples such as Solaris Paper's tripled gas bill and Advance Bricks' closure after gas prices rose from $6 to $37 per gigajoule.

The National Reconstruction Fund Corporation Bill 2023 creates a $15 billion government financing vehicle to invest in seven priority manufacturing areas—including renewables, medical science, and transport—through loans, equity, and guarantees. Supporters argued it will revive domestic manufacturing and secure jobs, while opponents criticised it as a fiscally irresponsible slush fund that ignores rising energy costs and regulatory burdens, with the Coalition and crossbenchers opposing the bill and the Greens securing amendments to prohibit funding for coal, gas, and native forest logging.

Argued that the National Reconstruction Fund Corporation Bill 2023 should support high-value Australian manufacturing, exclude fossil fuel and native forest logging, provide stable strategic direction and include relevant board expertise. Speakers discussed the $15 billion fund, electric vehicle manufacturing, Tasmanian forestry and Hydrowood, possible overlap with existing funds, and proposed amendments concerning investment eligibility.

The chair put second reading amendments to the National Reconstruction Fund Corporation Bill 2023: a Greens amendment from Senator Whish-Wilson, Senator David Pocock’s amendment calling for extra startup finance mechanisms and an ACT office for the Corporation, and Senator Thorpe’s amendment requiring free, prior and informed consent of First Nations Traditional Owners for major projects, reflected in the investment mandate and with close engagement. The Thorpe amendment was negatived, after which the main second reading question was put.

The government moved amendments to the National Reconstruction Fund Corporation Bill 2023 requiring the board to consider Australia’s greenhouse gas emissions reduction targets, decarbonisation, secure jobs, supply chain resilience and commercialisation of innovation, and to develop policies on environmental, labour, social and governance matters. The fund aims to create secure, well-paid manufacturing jobs—nearly 85% of manufacturing jobs are full-time—and will not fund coal, gas extraction or native forest logging.

The National Reconstruction Fund Corporation Bill passed the Senate, with Senator Farrell arguing it is one of the largest investments in Australian manufacturing history, providing finance to priority areas like agriculture, resources, transport, medical science, renewable energy, and defence. He stated amendments would attract private investment, reduce emissions, create secure jobs, and strengthen supply chains, while criticising the coalition for opposing the jobs and local manufacturing the fund aims to create.
